title: A spinning black-and-white disc makes you see colours that aren’t on it

cover.alt: Benham’s disc, white on one half and black on the other with sets of curved black arcs, beside the hand-cranked gold wheel that spins it.

body: Spin a disc printed only in black and white and many people see pale arcs of colour drift across it. These are **Fechner colours**, also called pattern-induced flicker colours: Gustav Fechner and Hermann von Helmholtz described them, and in 1895 the English toymaker Charles Benham sold a top painted with the pattern. Nothing on the disc is coloured. The colours seem to come from how neurons in the retina and the primary visual cortex respond to fast black-and-white flicker, and research points to the blue–yellow channel of colour vision.

slides.alt: A white disc, half black and marked with curved black arcs, sits beside a gold wheel linked to it by a red rubber band. A hand turns the wheel’s crank and the disc spins faster and faster.
slides.caption: A hand cranks a wheel whose rubber band spins Charles Benham’s 1895 disc. Watch the blur: many viewers see faint colours in it, though the disc is only black and white.

slides.prompt: Which everyday machine can show the same ghostly colours, but only while it speeds up or slows down?
slides.answer: A fan, especially one with aluminium blades
slides.detail: As the fan accelerates or decelerates, colours appear, drift, change and disappear. At its steady running speed it normally shows none.

steps.label: Fast flicker sweeps across the retina
Retina and visual cortex respond to it

slides.heading: A toy that became a test
slides.text: Charles Benham, a newspaperman and amateur scientist, was inspired by letters with Gustav Fechner, who had reported the colours in German, and his top brought the effect to English speakers. Researchers have since studied it as a way to detect diseases of the eye and visual pathway, with promise for optic neuritis.

slides.question: Which part of colour vision does research link to these flicker colours?
slides.explanation: Studies suggest a blue–yellow opponent process accounts for all the different pattern-induced flicker colours. They start in the retina and the primary visual cortex, not on the disc.
